Cirer les bottes de quelqu’un, le flatter obséquieusement. → voir lécher

examples.text: — Travailler avec Monsieur Coffe m’ôte tout appétit à dîner. C’est un parfait honnête homme, mais sa vue me cire.

glosses: allmählich größer werden; von der Größe, vom Umfang her zunehmen

examples.text: Kleine Kinder wachsen schnell.
„Er wurde in dieser Zeit noch einsamer, und er wurde immer aggressiver, denn seine Angst wuchs.“
Seine beiden Hunde sind in letzter Zeit ziemlich gewachsen.
Das rasant wachsende Unkraut muss gejätet werden.

glosses: sich im Laufe des Wachsens^([1]) entwickeln; an einer bestimmten Stelle vorkommen und gedeihen

examples.text: Maiglöckchen wachsen im Wald.
Diese Baumart wächst auf feuchtem Boden am besten.
Im Wald wachsen viele Beeren.

glosses: im Laufe der Zeit länger werden; an Länge gewinnen

examples.text: Seine Fingernägel wachsen schnell.
An Karls Hinterhaupt wachsen noch einige Haare, ansonsten ist er kahl.

glosses: sich in gewisser Weise im Wachstum entwickeln

examples.text: Der Baum muss beschnitten werden, denn er wächst bereits in den Garten meines Nachbarn.
Meine Pflanze ist fast bis an die Decke gewachsen.
Die Tanne ist schief gewachsen.

glosses: in der Größe, in der Menge, im Ausmaß steigen

examples.text: Das Vermögen des Milliardärs wächst stetig.
Die Stadt ist in den letzten Jahren stark gewachsen.
Ziel ist es, die wachsende Arbeitslosenquote zu bekämpfen.
Die wachsende Zahl an Infektionen deutet auf eine Durchseuchung hin.
„So wuchs das Feld der Starter zwar Jahr um Jahr, aber zunächst sehr langsam.“

glosses: von der Stärke, von der Bedeutung her zunehmen

examples.text: „Am schnellsten wächst der Einfluss des Islam. Das heißt, in globaler Perspektive kann man überhaupt nicht vom Verschwinden der Religion reden.“
„Aber der immer wachsende Lärm wurde bald so grell und furchtbar, daß er glaubte, die ganze Hölle sei los.“
„Sie sind motivierter, beschäftigen sich immer intensiver damit und Ihre Begeisterung wächst.“
„Der Frieden wächst, wie Rosen blühn, so bunt, so schön, so still.“

glosses: mit Wachs behandeln

examples.text: Die Möbel wurden nicht lackiert, sondern gewachst.
„Er knabberte nämlich gern an einer rohen Möhre, nachdem er das Auto gewachst und poliert hatte.“

translations.source_sense_description: Enduire ou frotter de cire.

glosses: Wurzeln im Untergrund schlagen

examples.text: Die Farne wuchsen in den verrottenden Holzkörper ein.

glosses: langsam von etwas (zum Beispiel Fleisch oder Gestein) umgeben werden

examples.text: Der Zehnagel wächst dann schnell mal ein und das tut weh.
Einzelne Kristalle sind in den Quarz eingewachsen.

glosses: mit Wachs bestreichen/belegen, in Wachs tränken

examples.text: Die Hausfrau hatte das Parkett frisch eingewachst.

glosses: Beeswax.
Earwax.

examples.text: What role does the wax in your earhole fulfill?

glosses: Any oily, water-resistant, solid or semisolid substance; normally long-chain hydrocarbons, alcohols or esters.
Any preparation containing wax, used as a polish.
The phonograph record format for music.

examples.text: What really started the corn sprouting on Broadway was a lugubrious tune by Louisiana's Jimmie Davis called It Makes No Difference Now. In the late '30s Decca's Recording Chief David Kapp heard this Texas hit and got it on wax.

glosses: A thick syrup made by boiling down the sap of the sugar maple and then cooling it.
Any of a class of drugs with weed oil and butane as main ingredients; hash oil.

examples.text: He was charged with two felonies, for possession of Xanax and wax.

glosses: Made of wax.

examples.text: He looked round the poor room, at the distempered walls, and the bad engravings in meretricious frames, the crinkly paper and wax flowers on the chiffonier; and he thought of a room like Father Bryan's, with panelling, with cut glass, with tulips in silver pots, such a room as he had hoped to have for his own.

glosses: To coat with wax or a similar material.

examples.text: waxed silk

glosses: To apply wax to (something, such as a shoe, a floor, a car, or an apple), usually to make it shiny.
To remove hair at the roots from (a part of the body) by coating the skin with a film of wax that is then pulled away sharply.
To defeat utterly.
To kill, especially to murder a person.

examples.text: "I was reassigned over from the 9th when the battalion CO got waxed on the road leading in." Ben kept his dismay to himself. Here was one more officer in the 90th who'd been on the job only hours or days, replacing commanders killed or wounded....

"You telling me you know who really waxed him and your mom?"
 "Yeah," she lied.
 "Just who pulled the trigger or who ordered it to be pulled?"

glosses: To record.
To greaten.

examples.text: Holonym: wax and wane

And then the whole quire hold their hips and laugh,
 And waxen in their mirth and neeze and swear
 A merrier hour was never wasted there.

For nature, crescent, does not grow alone
 In thews and bulks, but, as this temple waxes, The inward service of the mind and soul
 Grows wide withal.

And so it had always pleased M. Stutz to expect great things from the dark young man whom he had first seen in his early twenties ; and his expectations had waxed rather than waned on hearing the faint bruit of the love of Ivor and Virginia—for Virginia, M. Stutz thought, would bring fineness to a point in a man like Ivor Marlay, […].

glosses: To increasingly assume the specified characteristic.

examples.text: to wax poetic
to wax wode
to wax eloquent

Ah, ſirrah, by my ſay, it waxes late:
 I’ll to my reſt.
He waxes desperate with imagination.
As a cage is full of birds, so are their houses full of deceit: therefore they are become great, and waxen rich.
You behold, Sir, how he waxeth Wroth at your Abode here.
The stars grew pale and paler still till at last they vanished; the golden moon waxed wan, and her mountain ridges stood out against her sickly face.
In the night, or the gloomy chambers of the day, fears and misgivings wax strong, but out in the sunlight there is, for a time, cessation even of the terror of death.

glosses: To appear larger each night as a progression from a new moon to a full moon.
To move from low tide to high tide.
The process of growing.
An outburst of anger, a loss of temper, a fit of rage.

examples.text: father Arnall's face looked very black but he was not in a wax: he was laughing.
‘That's him to a T,’ she would murmur; or, ‘Just wait till he reads this’; or, ‘Ah, won't that put him in a wax!’

glosses: A substance used to polish.

examples.text: A good silver polish will remove tarnish easily.

glosses: Cleanliness; smoothness, shininess.

examples.text: The floor was waxed to a high polish.

glosses: Refinement; cleanliness in performance or presentation.

examples.text: The lecturer showed a lot of polish at his last talk.

glosses: To shine; to make a surface very smooth or shiny by rubbing, cleaning, or grinding.

examples.text: He polished up the chrome until it gleamed.

glosses: To refine; remove imperfections from.

examples.text: The band has polished its performance since the last concert.
Study gives strength to the mind; conversation, grace: the first apt to give stiffness, the other suppleness: one gives substance and form to the statue, the other polishes it.

glosses: To apply shoe polish to shoes.
To become smooth, as from friction; to receive a gloss; to take a smooth and glossy surface.

examples.text: Steel polishes well.
The other [gold], whether it will polish so well Wherein for the latter [brass] it is probable it will

glosses: To refine; to wear off the rudeness, coarseness, or rusticity of; to make elegant and polite.

examples.text: Arts that polish Life.
